abstract_paraphrase: The pathe of the ancient Greeks differ in partly systematic ways from modern emotions because they are grounded in the social world of the classical city-state. Against the neo-Darwinian basic-emotions program (Ekman, evolutionary psychology), Konstan argues that pathe are not internal states of excitation but COGNITIVE acts: construals of the words, acts, and intentions of others as they bear on one's social standing. He reads Aristotle's Rhetoric II.1 definition (emotions are what make people change/differ in their judgments, attended by pain and pleasure) as picking out emotion by its effect on krisis, and defends it via the De Anima I.1 form/matter (dialektikos/phusikos) distinction. Two corollaries are load-bearing: (1) animals and small children lack pathe 'in the proper sense' because emotion depends on the capacity for symbolization and is changeable by persuasion (analogical usage for beasts; Konstan rejects Nussbaum's ascription of emotion to animals); (2) grief did NOT fit Aristotle's conception of a pathos, since it lacks the relational/intentional structure (judgment of an agent's act, appraisal of desert/status) and the 'action readiness' shared by the genuine pathe, so grief may not qualify as a pathos at all. Per-emotion definitions: anger = desire for perceived revenge for a perceived slight (oligoria) by those not fit to slight; hatred = aim at harm, not painful; shame (aiskhune) = pain at disgrace-tending ills (act + character-flaw + loss of community esteem); phthonos = pain at an equal's success irrespective of desert or need (the only unqualifiedly negative pathos); to nemesan/nemesis = pain at undeserved good fortune (judgment of desert); fear = pain from a phantasia of a near future destructive evil, supposition-laden (Konstan sides with Andronicus's hupolepsis over Aspasius's bare phantasia); pity = pain at undeserved harm to one like oneself, when near.

outline.summary: Preface / thesis statement. Greek emotions differ from ours; the difference illuminates Greek literature and modern emotion theory. Romantic jealousy has no Greek term; grief 'did not fit Aristotle's conception of an emotion.' KEYSTONE (xii-xiii): animals and small children lack pathe 'in the proper sense' because emotions are elicited by our interpretation of others' words/acts/intentions and can be altered by changing the construal — impossible with dogs/infants; 'the emotions, as opposed to drives and appetites, depend on the capacity for symbolization'; persuasion is central to the idea of an emotion.

Ch. 1 Pathos and Passion — the theory. Lexical range of pathos (paschein; Met. 1022b15; De Mem. 449b4). Anti-universalist colour-terminology analogy (blue/indigo/glaukos/glas; J. Lyons; Lutz on Ifaluk fago). Critique of Darwin/Ekman/evolutionary psychology (fixation on expression/terminus; photography; Cartesian-Romantic private self). The cognitive turn (Lyons, Lazarus, Solomon, Nussbaum) converges on Aristotle (Fortenbaugh). Endorses Fortenbaugh's animal-restriction (quotes 2002:94 — analogical usage); rejects Nussbaum's ascription of emotion to animals (n.32). Flags human startle/'pre-emotions' (snake-stick, LeDoux dual pathway) as possibly sub-emotional. Social-relational turn (Manstead & Fischer; interdependent vs independent self; Elster). DEFINITION (Rhet. II.1 1378a20-23): emotions = what makes people change/differ in judgments, attended by pain+pleasure. Glosses both clauses (no valence-sorting; effect-on-judgment central, contra Fortenbaugh's 'local definition'). Defends via De Anima I.1 403a29-b2 form/matter (dialektikos/phusikos). Self-validating feedback loop (belief charged with pleasure/pain modifies/reinforces further beliefs; Aeneas's furor). Scope: pathe target agents, involve 'awareness of other subjectivities'; moods/appetites/sadness/loneliness/grief excluded.

Ch. 2 Anger. Definition (Rhet. II.2 1378a31-33): desire, accompanied by pain, for perceived revenge, for a perceived slight (oligoria) by people not fit to slight one or one's own. Centrality of evaluation/appraisal of social roles. Anger vs hatred (misos): hatred not painful, aims at harm/destruction, can target a group, is settled; anger painful, aims at the other's pain, requires the revenge be perceived (antipathein), is personal and time-healed. oligoria restriction: anger NOT a response to harm as such. Three species of slight: kataphronesis (contempt), epereasmos (spite), hubris (insolence/shaming for pleasure, from superiority). Hierarchical honour-world; slight from inferiors/no-account before valued others. Summary (75): self-esteem depends on social interaction; a public slight = lost credit; 'anger is precisely the desire to adjust the record' via compensatory revenge. [Homeric menis/cholos case-study not summarized.]

Ch. 4 Shame. aidos (prospective/inhibitory, self-image, Cairns) vs aiskhune (both prospective and retrospective; the pathos Aristotle analyses in the Rhetoric). Definition: pain/disturbance at disgrace-tending ills (adoxia), past/present/future. Konstan reads aiskhune as UNITARY (only the timing of the ills varies), dissolving the lexicographers' shame/sense-of-shame split. Three elements (101): the act (throwing away one's shield), the character-flaw revealed (cowardice), the loss of esteem before the community. Bridges modern shame/guilt divide. No Greek term for positive 'pride' (competitive polis: preserving status under the critical gaze, not basking in admiration). Shame symptomatic of a reputation-society.

Ch. 5 Envy and Indignation. to nemesan/nemesis = pain at undeserved success (Rhet. II.9 1386b8-9); opposite of pity (undeserved misfortune); both mark good character via a JUDGMENT OF DESERT (ascribed to gods). phthonos = pain at an equal's apparent success in goods, NOT to have the thing oneself, indifferent to BOTH desert AND need (Rhet. II.10 1387b23-25); the ONLY unqualifiedly negative pathos; mark of mikropsukhos/philodoxos. THESIS: 'indignation' (to nemesan) was not commonly an independent emotion in Aristotle's time — nemesis was archaic; pity/phthonos contrast prevailed afterward (Stoics, Cicero). Aristotle INTRODUCED/systematized to nemesan for systematic reasons (EE 1233b16-34: nemesetikos as mean between phthonos and epikhairekakia). Clearest case of the catalogue diverging from ordinary usage under philosophical pressure.

Ch. 6 Fear. Fear seems the universal, animal-shared emotion (deer in flight), testing cognitivism. Definition (Rhet. II.5 1382a21-25): pain/disturbance from a phantasia of a near future destructive/painful evil. Fear involves knowledge and inference: not pain but its portents frighten (snake, spear, snake-track/semeia). Aspasius (emotions from bare phantasiai/perception, prior to supposition) vs Andronicus (emotion from a hupolepsis/supposition of good/bad); KONSTAN SIDES WITH ANDRONICUS for fear and the other Rhetoric emotions (132). Fear socially conditioned: the frightening = hostile agents (anger/enmity) WITH power to harm, so fearing presupposes understanding anger/hatred. Fortenbaugh's soldier (dust-cloud inferred hostile; logos; 'fear makes men deliberate' Rhet. 1385a5; 'logos in which animals have no share'). Confidence (to tharsos) rests on inference about relative strength. Thucydides/Aeschylus: fear grounded-in and colouring judgment, rhetorically manipulable (alter 'perception of the enemy's capabilities,' enacting II.1).

Ch. 10 Pity. eleos NOT an instinctive response to pain but depends on a JUDGMENT of whether suffering is deserved; 'both cognitive and social,' moral appraisals. Definition (Rhet. II.8 1385b13-16): pain at an apparent destructive/painful harm of one not deserving it, which one might expect oneself or one's own to suffer, when near. The 'distance' condition: recognize resemblance to the sufferer yet not share the plight (complete identification != pity). Konstan WIDENS eleos: room in Aristotle's scheme for humane sensibility toward even an undeserving sufferer via the 'common laws of the Greeks' setting limits on legitimate suffering (Plataean appeals, Thucydides/Isocrates). Retains the for-whom/toward-whom structure.

Ch. 12 Grief — the pathos-status problem. Grief (lupe/penthos) named and ritualized (lamentation, consolation genre) but ABSENT from the Rhetoric catalogue. Lexical explanation: lupe = Aristotle's word for 'pain,' a constituent SENSATION (aisthesis) of pathe, not itself a pathos. SUBSTANTIVE argument (247-248): grief 'involves no judgment of intentions, no reckoning of relative power, no reference to desert or to social status'; loss strikes with immediacy 'as if the fact itself were painful' — 'in this sense, the grieving is like physical pain.' Grief lacks 'action readiness': no compensatory act, no responsible agent, 'no one to get even with'; only time heals. KEYSTONE (248): the pathe are social, responses to behaviour by conscious agents, enmeshed in competitive honour/esteem (doxa); a pathos is a 'social transaction'; 'the natural fact of death stands outside this system.' Sophocles' Electra: her driving passion is ANGER/vengeance (father murdered), not 'passive grief elicited by a morally neutral event' — anger has the agency/action-readiness/social dimension grief lacks. Verdict (258): grief and anger 'look radically different, even to the point that grief might not qualify as a pathos at all.'

Conclusion. Precis of the social reading: Aristotle's emotional world is highly competitive, everyone jockeying for social position, conscious of standing in others' eyes. zelos/emulation, anger, shame, fear, pity, indignation each tuned to relative standing, power, desert, the gaze of others. The Greek 'ideological construction of the emotions' differs from ours partly because moderns treat emotions as interior feelings rather than responses to social interaction.

concepts.label: pathos as cognitive judgment / appraisal (not internal excitation)
concepts.gloss: Greek pathe are acts of judgment — construals of events — not states of excitation; emotions essentially involve a substantial cognitive component (Ch.1, 23-24, 33).

concepts.label: the social-relational / toward-whom structure of emotion
concepts.gloss: pathe are responses to the acts/intentions of conscious agents bearing on one's social standing; they 'involve an awareness of other subjectivities' and are 'social transactions,' each with a built-in for-whom and against-whom (39-40, 248).

concepts.label: emotion as changeable by persuasion (rhetoric changes the construal)
concepts.gloss: because a pathos rests on how one construes the precipitating event, altering the construal (showing a slight was unintended) alters the emotion; persuasion is central to the idea of an emotion (xii, 35).

concepts.label: the Rhetoric II.1 definition: effect on judgment + pain/pleasure
concepts.gloss: pathe = 'all those things on account of which people change and differ in regard to their judgments, and upon which attend pain and pleasure' (1378a20-23); picks out emotion by its effect on krisis, not by its cause (27, 33-35).

concepts.label: animals and small children lack pathe 'in the proper sense'
concepts.gloss: emotion depends on the capacity for symbolization/judgment and is reachable by persuasion; beasts/infants are not, so beast-applications of orge/phobos are ANALOGICAL usage (Preface xii; 22, quoting Fortenbaugh 2002:94).

concepts.label: Konstan's demurral: emotion (and judgment) NOT ascribed to animals (contra Nussbaum)
concepts.gloss: a difficulty with Nussbaum's extreme cognitivism is that she ascribes emotions, hence judgment, to animals; Konstan sides with the rationality-restriction (23, n.32).

concepts.label: grief did not fit Aristotle's conception of a pathos
concepts.gloss: grief is absent from the Rhetoric and lacks the relational/intentional structure (no judgment of intentions, desert, or status) and 'action readiness' of the genuine pathe; 'grief might not qualify as a pathos at all' (245-248, 258).

concepts.label: lupe = 'pain' as a constituent sensation (aisthesis) of pathe, not a pathos
concepts.gloss: the most common Greek word for grief is also Aristotle's word for pain, one of the two aistheseis that are COMPONENTS of (not identical with) an emotion — so grief is hard to rank alongside the other pathe (245-246).

concepts.label: 'action readiness' as a mark of the genuine pathe
concepts.gloss: the genuine emotions carry an answering disposition (anger->revenge, love->the other's good, envy/zelos->equality); grief invites no compensatory act and has no responsible agent — 'no one to get even with' (247-248).

concepts.label: anger = desire for perceived revenge for a perceived slight (oligoria)
concepts.gloss: Rhet. II.2 1378a31-33; oligoria (belittlement) is the SOLE cause; anger aims at the other's pain and requires the revenge be perceived; restores diminished social standing (41-46, 75).

concepts.label: three species of slight: kataphronesis, epereasmos, hubris
concepts.gloss: contempt (active belief a thing is worthless), spite (thwarting another's wishes for no gain of one's own), insolence/abuse (shaming another for the sheer pleasure of superiority) (45-46).

concepts.label: anger vs hatred (orge vs misos)
concepts.gloss: hatred is not painful, aims at harm/destruction, can target a class, and is settled/lasting; anger is painful, aims at the other's felt diminishment, is personal, and heals with time (42, 47-48).

concepts.label: shame (aiskhune) as a unitary pathos: act + character-flaw + loss of community esteem
concepts.gloss: Rhet. II.6; pain at disgrace-tending ills (adoxia) past/present/future; three elements (the act, the vice it reveals, the loss of esteem); only the timing varies, dissolving the shame/sense-of-shame split (98-102).

concepts.label: aidos vs aiskhune (prospective-inhibitory vs the retrospective-capable pathos)
concepts.gloss: aidos is prospective/inhibitory, an inhibitory emotion of self-image (Cairns), 'not shame'; aiskhune is the affect Aristotle analyses as a pathos in the Rhetoric (93-96).

concepts.label: phthonos (envy) — pain at an equal's success, indifferent to desert AND need; the only unqualifiedly negative pathos
concepts.gloss: Rhet. II.10 1387b23-25; not to have the thing oneself but on the other's account; mark of the mikropsukhos/philodoxos; the only pathos Aristotle treats as wholly negative (112-113).

concepts.label: to nemesan / nemesis (indignation) — pain at undeserved good fortune; judgment of desert
concepts.gloss: Rhet. II.9 1386b8-9; opposite of pity; marks good character via an assessment of fairness/desert; ascribed to the gods (112).

concepts.label: Aristotle's catalogue can diverge from ordinary Greek usage under systematic pressure
concepts.gloss: 'indignation' (to nemesan) was not a common independent emotion; Aristotle appropriated an archaic word (nemesis) to supply a noun answering to the vice phthonos (EE 1233b16-34) — the catalogue is partly a philosophical construct (111-115).

concepts.label: fear (phobos) = pain from a phantasia of a near future destructive evil; supposition-laden
concepts.gloss: Rhet. II.5 1382a21-25; fear involves knowledge and inference (portents/semeia frighten, not pain itself); Konstan sides with Andronicus's hupolepsis over Aspasius's bare phantasia for the Rhetoric emotions (130-132).

concepts.label: Aspasius vs Andronicus on the cognition in emotion (bare phantasia vs hupolepsis)
concepts.gloss: Aspasius: certain emotions arise from bare phantasiai (perception), prior to any supposition; Andronicus: emotion arises from a supposition (hupolepsis) of good/bad; Konstan judges the truth lies 'more with Andronicus' for fear and the other Rhetoric emotions (132). [Maps onto the cluster's DOXASTIC<->PHANTASTIC axis.]

concepts.label: fear is socially conditioned (hostile agents WITH power to harm)
concepts.gloss: the frightening par excellence are agents who are hostile and able to harm; fearing therefore presupposes understanding anger/hatred, which depend on complex judgments; confidence rests on inference about relative strength (132-133).

concepts.label: pity (eleos) — pain at undeserved harm to one like oneself; the 'distance' condition
concepts.gloss: Rhet. II.8 1385b13-16; depends on a judgment of desert and on recognizing resemblance to the sufferer WITHOUT sharing the plight (complete identification != pity); cognitive and social (201-202).

concepts.label: the form/matter (dialektikos/phusikos) defense of the Rhetoric definition
concepts.gloss: De Anima I.1 403a29-b2: the dialectician defines anger by its form/logos ('a desire to return pain for pain'), the natural scientist by its matter (blood around the heart); the Rhetoric definition is of the formal/teleological kind — what emotions are 'used for' (35-37).

concepts.label: the self-validating emotion / circular cognitive system (the pathetic loop)
concepts.gloss: a belief charged with pleasure/pain modifies further beliefs and can reinforce the original judgment, making emotions 'self-validating' and hard to eradicate — 'a closed or circular cognitive system' (37-38).

concepts.label: anti-universalism: the emotional lexicon is culturally constructed (colour-terminology analogy)
concepts.gloss: as colour terms (blue/indigo/glaukos/glas) carve the spectrum differently across languages, so emotion-vocabularies differ; the Greek pathe-list exhibits mergings, hiatuses, and intersections against modern catalogues (5-16).

concepts.label: the honour/esteem (time, doxa) world as the ground of the pathe
concepts.gloss: Aristotle's emotional world is hierarchical and competitive (Elster: 'everybody knows that they are constantly being judged'); self-esteem depends on social interaction; the pathe are tuned to relative standing (24, 73-75, 259-261).

concepts.label: human 'pre-emotions' (startle) may be sub-emotional / merely analogous to emotion
concepts.gloss: the snake-stick recoil (LeDoux's dual subcortical/cortical pathway) is an automatism analogous to fear; genuine fear requires the autonomic response 'in synch with a particular learned response,' so startle alone is not yet an emotion (25-27).

readings.thesis: The Greek pathe are cognitive acts — construals of others' acts/intentions bearing on social standing — not internal states of excitation; emotion is constitutively SOCIAL/relational.

The Rhetoric II.1 definition (emotion = what changes/differs people's judgments, attended by pain/pleasure) is Aristotle's real definition of emotion, not a context-local one, and is defensible via the De Anima I.1 form/matter (dialektikos) account.

Aristotle (and the Greek philosophers) held that animals and small children do NOT have pathe 'in the proper sense'; beast-applications of orge/phobos are analogical. Konstan rejects Nussbaum's ascription of emotion/judgment to animals.

Grief (lupe/penthos) did not fit Aristotle's conception of a pathos: it lacks the relational/intentional structure (no judgment of intentions, desert, or status) and the 'action readiness' shared by the genuine pathe; 'grief might not qualify as a pathos at all.'
loci: Rhet. II (grief absent from the catalogue)
readings.axis: T1-4: emotions toward non-realizable goods (DIRECTLY relevant; the dissertation's primary witness)

readings.thesis: Anger is a desire for perceived revenge for a perceived slight (oligoria) by those not fit to slight one; it is NOT a response to harm as such (that is hatred), but a response to a status-diminishing belittlement, answered by a compensatory act that restores social standing.
readings.axis: social-relational construal of a single emotion (the toward-whom paradigm)

readings.thesis: For fear and the other Rhetoric emotions the constitutive cognition is a SUPPOSITION (hupolepsis), siding with Andronicus over Aspasius's bare-phantasia view — a witness AGAINST the phantasia-only reading.

Aiskhune is a UNITARY emotion (pain at disgrace-tending ills, only the timing varying), with three elements — act, character-flaw revealed, loss of community esteem — that bridge the modern shame/guilt divide.
readings.axis: the social/communal individuation of an emotion

readings.thesis: Aristotle's catalogue is partly a philosophical CONSTRUCT that can diverge from ordinary Greek usage: 'indignation' (to nemesan) was not a common independent emotion; Aristotle systematized it (with archaic nemesis) to answer the vice phthonos.
readings.axis: how far the Rhetoric list reflects usage vs system (caution for the dissertation)

readings.thesis: The role of evaluation in emotion is not merely constitutive but DYNAMIC: an emotion-grounding belief, charged with pleasure/pain, modifies and can reinforce further beliefs, yielding a self-validating, circular cognitive system.
readings.axis: the pathetic-loop / emotion->belief feedback (synchronic/diachronic status left open)

aes_internal: aes-01 Fortenbaugh: ENDORSED throughout (the cognitivist reading, 22-23, 31, 43; quotes the 2002 epilogue p.94 on animals/analogical usage; but DISPUTES Fortenbaugh 2002:114 that the Rhetoric II.1 definition is merely context-local, 35; cites Fortenbaugh 2003-4 on 'family resemblance,' 27-28); Konstan thanks Fortenbaugh in the Acknowledgments
opposes: aes-03 / aes-04 Moss (non-judgmental / phantastic): by implication via Konstan's siding with Andronicus's hupolepsis over Aspasius's bare phantasia for the Rhetoric emotions (132); the cluster's clearest classicist witness against a phantasia-only reading
congenial: aes-05 Dow (affirmation/judgmental): Konstan's social-appraisal model is congenial to Dow's belief/affirmation reading, though pitched at cultural-semantic content rather than the assent-vs-appearance metaphysics; both range on the judgmental pole
cross_pipeline: Phantasia Secondary cluster: fear's phantasia (Rhet. II.5 1382a21) and the Aspasius/Andronicus dispute bear on phantasia-as-appearance vs phantasia-as-supposition; Heidegger BCAP: pathos as being-with-others / doxa as the public taking-as (Mitsein); Gross Uncomfortable Situations 2017 (situated/social emotion); Corcilius (non-rational pleasure/pain/desire; animal motion) on the animal-pathos question

tensions.desc: Konstan's 'judgment' is SOCIAL APPRAISAL/construal, not doxa in Aristotle's technical taking-as-true sense; he is an ally of the judgmental pole on emotion=judgment while supplying a social-construal (not propositional-doxa) analysis of the judgment's content.

On fear Konstan sides with Andronicus's hupolepsis (supposition) AGAINST Aspasius's bare phantasia, yet Aristotle's own fear definition uses phantasia and concerns a FUTURE evil (not present pain); Konstan must read 'impression of a future evil' as supposition-laden, conceding Aristotle's wording leans phantastic (132).

Konstan endorses Fortenbaugh's cognitivism but rejects his claim that the Rhetoric II.1 definition is merely context-local (35), and rejects Nussbaum's animal-emotions while sharing her cognitivism — the cognitivist camp is internally split on scope (animals) and on whether the Rhetoric definition is general.

Grief 'might not qualify as a pathos at all' (258): an affect oriented to an irreversible/non-realizable state of affairs, lacking a responsible agent and action-readiness, falls outside the relational-intentional schema — the dissertation's primary witness and ready-made test for emotions toward non-realizable goods.

The pathe 'involve an awareness of other subjectivities' and are 'social transactions' (39, 248): the toward-whom / Mitsein structure (element 2) is constitutive, not incidental — the classicist confirmation that Aristotle's emotions are directed at others' acts/intentions bearing on standing.

Animals/children lack pathe 'in the proper sense' (xii, 22); beast-emotion is analogical usage; Konstan rejects Nussbaum's animal-ascription — strong support for the dissertation's restriction of pathe 'in the proper sense' to rational/judging/social beings (on a social-judgmental, not phantasia-based, rationale).

dissertation_hooks.element-2-toward-whom-Mitsein: PRIMARY: the classicist witness that the pathe are constitutively relational ('awareness of other subjectivities'; 'social transactions'); each emotion has a built-in for-whom/against-whom (anger's offender, pity's 'oneself or one's own,' shame's community, fear's hostile agent). Anchors: Rhet. II.2 1378a31-33, II.8 1385b13-16; Konstan 24, 30-31, 39-40, 248.
dissertation_hooks.animal-pathos: Animals and small children lack pathe 'in the proper sense' (Preface xii; Ch.1 22-23); beast-applications of orge/phobos are analogical; Konstan rejects Nussbaum's animal-emotions (23 n.32). Strong support for the rational-only restriction, on a social-judgmental rationale.
dissertation_hooks.T1-4-grief: DIRECTLY relevant primary witness: grief did not fit Aristotle's conception of a pathos — no judgment of intentions/desert/status, no action-readiness, no responsible agent; 'grief might not qualify as a pathos at all' (245-248, 258). Supplies the explicit exclusion-criterion for emotions toward non-realizable goods.
dissertation_hooks.T1-2-doxa-vs-phantasia: ALLY of the judgmental side (emotion = judgment/appraisal) and a witness AGAINST the phantasia-only reading via the Aspasius/Andronicus verdict (sides with hupolepsis, 132). NUANCE: his 'judgment' is social construal/appraisal, not technical doxa — arms the upper tier of the two-tier reconciliation without by itself settling the doxa-gate. Also supplies the self-validating-emotion / pathetic-loop intuition (37-38).
